lessons.title: poner — "to put," and the club gains a member
lessons.gloss: to put / to place — a -go yo-form, pongo

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: In Chapter 12 you met the -go club — tengo, hago, digo — and three members "to come": pongo, salgo, vengo. Here is the first of them. poner ("to put / to place") is a plain -er verb everywhere except the yo-form, which grows the familiar g: pongo.
g-hard — the g in pongo is the hard -go you now know from tengo.
poner comes from Latin pōnere, "to put, to place, to set down" — and its stem pon-/pos- ("place") is one of the busiest roots in English:
position, pose, posit — a placing.
with prefixes: compose ("place together"), deposit ("place down"), expose ("place out"), oppose / opponent ("place against"), propose ("place forward"), postpone ("place after"), component, deposit.
So poner and position share the same "place" root — you are putting something in its pōnere.
Only the yo-form is irregular — it takes the g — the rest is a regular -er present:
The everyday payoff: poner la mesa ("to set the table"), poner música ("to put on music"), and the reflexive ponerse — "to put on (clothes)" or "to become" (me pongo nervioso, "I get nervous").

lessons.title: Practice — the -go club, complete
lessons.gloss: the whole -go club, complete — tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Chapter 12 opened the -go club with tengo, hago, digo; this chapter closed it with pongo, salgo, vengo. All six in one place now — say them until the yo-forms are automatic.
Say each infinitive, then its yo-form:
tener becomes tengo, hacer becomes hago, decir becomes digo.
poner becomes pongo, salir becomes salgo, venir becomes vengo.
What do all six yo-forms share? (The -go.) In which form only? (The yo-form — the rest is regular, plus any stem-change.)
Sort the club by how irregular:
plain -go (regular otherwise): hago, pongo, salgo.
-go + e becomes i (the decir type): digo (dices/dice).
-go + e becomes ie (the boot twins): tengo (tienes), vengo (vienes).

blocks.title: Drill 3 — run the two boot verbs

segments.text: Say tener and venir full — they are mirror twins:
tener: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.
venir: vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, vienen.
Only tenemos / venimos keep the plain e — the boot.
Say each out loud:
"Vengo de casa y pongo la mesa." — "I come from home and set the table."
"Salgo a las ocho." — "I leave at eight."
"¿Qué haces? — Hago la cena." — "What are you doing? — I'm making dinner."
"Digo que sí." — "I say yes."

blocks.title: Drill 5 — the root families (say the cousin)

segments.text: One English cousin each:
poner from pōnere becomes? (position / compose / deposit.)
salir from salīre becomes? (salient / salmon / somersault.)
venir from venīre becomes? (adventure / event / convene.)

Recite the six yo-forms of the club. (tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo.) Which two are the e becomes ie "boot" twins? (tener and venir.) Which single verb is -go and e becomes i? (decir — digo/dices.) You now hold the whole irregular -go corner of Spanish — its oldest, most-used verbs, mastered as one pattern.

lessons.title: salir — "to go out," from a verb that meant "to leap"
lessons.gloss: to leave / to go out — a -go yo-form, salgo, from a root that means "to leap"

segments.text: The second -go verb: salir ("to leave, to go out"). Same story as poner — regular -ir everywhere but the yo-form, which grows the g: salgo. But its origin is a delight: salir comes from a Latin verb for leaping.
salir comes from Latin salīre, "to leap, to jump, to spring" — and over time "leaping out" softened into simply "going out." The leap survives across English:
salient ("leaping out," so: prominent, sticking out), sally ("a sudden rush out"), somersault (sopra + saltus, "a leap over").
with prefixes: assail / assault ("leap at"), resilient ("leap back"), result ("leap back out"), insult ("leap upon").
and the salmon — salīre gave Latin salmō, "the leaper," for the fish that leaps upstream.
So every time you say salgo ("I go out"), you are using the old "leap" verb behind salient and salmon.

The everyday payoff: salir de casa ("to leave the house"), salir con alguien ("to go out with someone" — to date), and la salida ("the exit" — the sign you'll read at every station). Note: English exit is from a different Latin verb, exīre ("go out"); Spanish chose the leaping one.

lessons.title: venir — "to come," the last club member, cracked and g-grown
lessons.gloss: to come — doubly irregular, vengo + e becomes ie, completing the -go club

segments.text: The sixth and final member of the -go club: venir ("to come"). And like decir back in Chapter 12, it is doubly irregular — it stacks the -go yo-form and a stem-change. Learn venir and the whole system you've been building since tener clicks shut.
g-hard — the -go of vengo.
diphthong-ie — the stressed stem e breaks to ie: vienes = vee-EH-nes.
venir comes from Latin venīre, "to come" — a root ven-/vent- that comes toward English from every direction:

adventure (ad-venīre, "what comes to you"), event ("what comes out"), convene / convention ("come together"), invent ("come upon"), prevent ("come before"), intervene, revenue ("what comes back"), avenue ("a coming-toward"), and souvenir (French, "a thing that comes to mind").

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two irregularities at once

segments.text: (1) The -go yo-form, like pongo/salgo/tengo: vengo. (2) The e becomes ie stem-change, like querer/tener: the stressed stem breaks to ie — the "boot" again.

Venimos alone keeps the plain e (stress on the ending), drawing the boot; everything inside it cracks to ie, and the yo corner carries the -go. This is the exact shape of tener (tengo / tienes) — venir is its mirror twin.
You have now met all six: tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo. Three plain -go (poner, salir, hacer), one -go + e becomes i (decir), two -go + e becomes ie (tener, venir). The corner is closed.
